hints: Look carefully at the y-axis. It is substrate concentration LEFT after 10 minutes, not the rate of reaction, so ask yourself what low remaining substrate tells you.
Recall the normal bell-shaped rate against temperature curve with an optimum, then think what the upside-down version of it would look like for substrate remaining.
walkthrough:
**Spot the trick in the y-axis**

This is the key to the whole question. You are not plotting rate, you are plotting how much substrate is still there after 10 minutes.

Remember this simple link:
$$\text{fast rate = lots of substrate used up = low substrate left}$$

**Predict low, optimum and high temperature**

At low temperature, kinetic energy is low, collisions are few, so rate is slow and lots of substrate remains. High remaining substrate.

At the optimum temperature, rate is fastest, so most substrate is used up in 10 minutes. Lowest remaining substrate.

**Add denaturation and pick the inverted curve**

Above the optimum, the enzyme denatures, active site shape is lost, so rate falls sharply to almost zero and substrate remains high again.

So as temperature rises, remaining substrate falls to a minimum then rises again. That is a U-shaped curve, which is graph D.

options.A: Shows substrate falling and staying low at high temperature. That would mean the enzyme keeps working fast after denaturation, which is incorrect.
options.B: Shows a peak of substrate at the optimum temperature. This is the shape for rate of reaction, not substrate left, so the logic is upside down.
options.C: Shows substrate remaining increasing all the way. That would mean rate keeps falling with temperature, with no optimum and no denaturation effect.
options.D: Correct U-shape. High substrate left when slow at low temperature, minimum left at optimum when fastest, then high left again when denatured at high temperature.
